title: Only build the services that actually changed
summary: A monorepo CI that rebuilds everything on every push wastes hours a day. Compute the changed paths from git, map them to services, and handle the two cases that break naive implementations.
mental_model: 'What changed' is `git diff --name-only <base>...<head>`. Everything else — which services to build, which tests to run — is a mapping from those paths. The hard part is choosing the right base, not the diffing.

steps.title: Change one service and ask git what moved
steps.why: `diff --name-only` against the base branch is the whole mechanism. Two dots would also include changes made on main since you branched — three dots compares against the merge base, which is what a CI job means by 'what this branch changed'.
steps.expect: One changed file, and only the payments service scheduled to build.

verify.label: only the changed service is built
verify.hint: git diff --name-only origin/main...HEAD, then map paths to services

steps.title: Prove the three-dot range matters
steps.why: Push an unrelated change to main, then compare. The two-dot diff now claims your branch touched the catalog service — which would rebuild it for no reason, on every branch, for the rest of the day.

actions.run: git commit -q -m "feat(catalog): unrelated work on main"

steps.expect: Two dots mentions catalog; three dots does not.

verify.label: the three-dot range shows only what the branch changed
…while the two-dot range wrongly blames the branch for main's work

steps.title: Docs changes should build nothing
steps.why: The mapping is where the value is: paths that cannot affect a build produce no jobs. This is usually the single biggest saving in a monorepo pipeline.

actions.run: git commit -q -m "docs: update the architecture diagram"

steps.expect: Still only payments — the docs change adds no jobs.

steps.title: A shared library must fan out
steps.why: The trap in the other direction. A change under `libs/` affects every consumer, so the mapping must expand it — otherwise CI passes and production breaks in a service nobody rebuilt.

actions.run: git commit -q -m "refactor(common): change the helper return type"

steps.expect: All three services scheduled, because they all depend on the library.

verify.label: a shared library change fans out to every consumer
verify.hint: map libs/* to all services, or CI will miss a broken consumer

steps.title: The failure mode that bites in CI
steps.why: In a shallow clone the base commit does not exist, so the diff fails or returns everything. `fetch-depth: 0` — or an explicit `git fetch origin main` — is the fix, and it is the commonest reason path filtering 'randomly' rebuilds the world.
steps.expect: The shallow clone cannot reach HEAD~1, so the diff fails outright.

steps.title: Compute the base the way CI should
steps.why: Fetch the base branch explicitly and use `merge-base`. This works on a shallow clone once the base is fetched, and it does not depend on any CI platform's variables.
commands: sh -c 'cd ../ci-shallow && git fetch -q --depth 50 origin main && git log --oneline | wc -l'
sh -c 'cd ../ci-shallow && git merge-base HEAD origin/main | head -c 8'
sh -c 'cd ../ci-shallow && git diff --name-only $(git merge-base HEAD origin/main)..HEAD | head -3'
steps.expect: A usable base and a correct changed-file list.

steps.title: Wire it into the pipeline
steps.why: Commit the mapping script so it is reviewed like any other code, and so the same logic runs locally and in CI. A pipeline whose filtering logic lives only in YAML cannot be tested before pushing.

actions.run: sh -c 'git commit -q -m "ci: build only the affected services" --allow-empty'

verify.label: the mapping is committed and testable locally
the branch's changed-file list excludes main's own work
verify.hint: use the three-dot range against the base branch

verify.label: the shared library change correctly fans out to all three services
every consumer of the changed library is scheduled
the path-to-service mapping lives in the repository

pitfalls: Two dots versus three dots decides whether main's own commits get attributed to your branch. In CI, always three — or an explicit merge-base.
Shallow clones break path filtering silently: the base is unreachable, the diff errors, and most pipelines fall back to building everything.
Forgetting to fan out shared-library changes is the dangerous direction: CI goes green and a consumer breaks in production.
A merge commit's diff against its first parent is not 'what this PR changed'. Use the merge base with the target branch instead.
Path filters in CI YAML cannot be tested locally. Putting the logic in a committed script means you can run it before you push.
cheatsheet: make the base reachable in CI
